title: The training loop
summary: Every model is trained by the same loop: a forward pass turns a mini-batch into predictions, the loss boils them down to one number, the backward pass computes a gradient for every parameter (same shape as the parameter), and the update moves each weight a little against its gradient. Steps repeat over shuffled data in epochs, while the loop logs training loss, checks validation loss without updating, and saves checkpoints.
llm_link: Pretraining a language model is this loop: inputs are batches of text, targets are the same text shifted by one token, the loss is cross-entropy on the next token, and the loop runs for a very large number of steps across many machines.
key_ideas: Forward pass: mini-batch → predictions → loss, one number averaged over the batch.
Backward pass: ∂L/∂w for every parameter, by the chain rule from the loss backwards; each gradient has the same shape as its weight.
Update: w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w. In PyTorch, gradients accumulate, so clear them (zero_grad) before each backward pass.
An epoch is one pass over every example; shuffle at the start of each epoch. Steps per epoch = ceil(N / batch size).
Log training loss, evaluate validation loss with no updates, and save checkpoints so you can resume and keep the best weights.

quiz.q: Predict the result: 1,000 training examples, batch size 50. How many update steps make one epoch?
quiz.explain: Each step uses one mini-batch of 50, so covering all 1,000 examples takes 1000 / 50 = 20 steps.

quiz.q: A weight matrix W has shape (128, 64). What is the shape of ∂L/∂W?
quiz.explain: There is one partial derivative per entry of W, so the gradient has exactly W's shape.

quiz.q: In PyTorch you forget to call optimizer.zero_grad() inside the loop. What happens?
options: Each step uses the sum of the current and all earlier gradients
quiz.explain: backward() adds into .grad. Without clearing, old gradients keep pushing every later step: the ghosts of earlier batches.

quiz.q: Why does the loop measure validation loss without updating the weights?
options: Updates on validation data would make it part of training, so it would no longer measure generalisation
quiz.explain: The validation set is only useful as an honest check on unseen data; training on it destroys that.

quiz.q: When a language model is pretrained, what are the targets for a batch of text?
options: The same text shifted by one token
quiz.explain: At every position the target is simply the next token, so the text supervises itself.

problems.title: Train a line with the loop
problems.prompt:
Write the whole training loop for pred = w * x + b with plain Python lists. Start from w = 0, b = 0. Each epoch, use all the data (one batch):

  1. forward: predictions and the mean squared error L = mean((pred - y)**2); append L to losses
  2. backward: dw = mean(2 * (pred - y) * x), db = mean(2 * (pred - y))
  3. update: w -= lr * dw, b -= lr * db

Return (w, b, losses).

xs = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]; ys = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]   # y = 2x + 1
train_line(xs, ys)   # w ≈ 2, b ≈ 1
problems.starter:
def train_line(xs, ys, lr=0.05, epochs=500):
    w, b = 0.0, 0.0
    losses = []
    n = len(xs)
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # TODO 1 forward: preds and loss (append to losses)
        # TODO 2 backward: dw and db
        # TODO 3 update: w and b
        pass
    return w, b, losses

tests.name: recovers y = 2x + 1
tests.code:
w, b, losses = train_line([0, 1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 3, 5, 7, 9])
assert abs(w - 2) < 0.05 and abs(b - 1) < 0.1, f'expected w ≈ 2, b ≈ 1, got w = {w:.3f}, b = {b:.3f}. Check the signs: subtract lr * gradient.'

tests.name: one loss per epoch, falling
tests.code:
w, b, losses = train_line([0, 1, 2, 3], [0, -1, -2, -3], epochs=100)
assert len(losses) == 100, f'append one loss per epoch: expected 100 values, got {len(losses)}'
assert losses[-1] < losses[0] * 0.01, f'loss should fall a lot: first {losses[0]:.3f}, last {losses[-1]:.3f}'

tests.name: first loss is measured before any update
tests.code:
w, b, losses = train_line([1, 2], [3, 5], epochs=1)
assert abs(losses[0] - 17.0) < 1e-9, f'with w = b = 0 the first loss is mean(3², 5²) = 17, got {losses[0] if losses else None}. Compute the loss in the forward pass, before updating.'

hints: preds = [w * x + b for x in xs]; errs = [p - y for p, y in zip(preds, ys)]
loss = sum(e * e for e in errs) / n; dw = sum(2 * e * x for e, x in zip(errs, xs)) / n; db = sum(2 * e for e in errs) / n
w -= lr * dw; b -= lr * db  (zip, not a nested loop)
problems.solution:
def train_line(xs, ys, lr=0.05, epochs=500):
    w, b = 0.0, 0.0
    losses = []
    n = len(xs)
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        preds = [w * x + b for x in xs]
        errs = [p - y for p, y in zip(preds, ys)]
        losses.append(sum(e * e for e in errs) / n)
        dw = sum(2 * e * x for e, x in zip(errs, xs)) / n
        db = sum(2 * e for e in errs) / n
        w -= lr * dw
        b -= lr * db
    return w, b, losses

problems.title: Mini-batches, epochs and shuffling (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Two functions for a logistic-regression classifier trained with mini-batches.

  • minibatches(n, batch_size, rng): shuffle the indices 0..n-1 with rng.permutation(n) and split them into consecutive chunks of batch_size (the last chunk may be smaller). Return a list of index arrays.
  • train_logreg(X, y, lr=0.5, epochs=30, batch_size=16, seed=0): start from w = zeros(d), b = 0; make rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); for each epoch, for each batch: p = sigmoid(Xb @ w + b), dw = Xb.T @ (p - yb) / len(yb), db = mean(p - yb), then update. After each epoch, append the full-data cross-entropy to history. Return (w, b, history).

tests.name: batches cover every example once
tests.code:
import numpy as np
bs = minibatches(50, 16, np.random.default_rng(1))
assert [len(b) for b in bs] == [16, 16, 16, 2], f'50 examples in batches of 16 should give sizes [16, 16, 16, 2], got {[len(b) for b in bs]}'
assert sorted(np.concatenate(bs).tolist()) == list(range(50)), 'every index 0..49 must appear exactly once per epoch'

tests.name: the order is shuffled
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
a = np.concatenate(minibatches(30, 10, rng)); b = np.concatenate(minibatches(30, 10, rng))
assert not np.array_equal(a, np.arange(30)), 'indices should be shuffled with rng.permutation, not left in order'
assert not np.array_equal(a, b), 'each epoch should draw a fresh shuffle'

tests.name: learns a separable problem
tests.code:
import numpy as np
r = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.vstack([r.normal(-1.5, 1, (100, 2)), r.normal(1.5, 1, (100, 2))]); y = np.r_[np.zeros(100), np.ones(100)]
w, b, hist = train_logreg(X, y)
acc = ((sigmoid(X @ w + b) > 0.5) == y).mean()
assert acc > 0.9, f'accuracy should exceed 0.9, got {acc:.2f}'
assert len(hist) == 30, f'one history value per epoch: expected 30, got {len(hist)}'
assert hist[-1] < hist[0], f'loss should fall: first {hist[0] if hist else None}, last {hist[-1] if hist else None}'

hints: idx = rng.permutation(n); return [idx[i:i + batch_size] for i in range(0, n, batch_size)]
After the batches: p = np.clip(sigmoid(X @ w + b), 1e-9, 1 - 1e-9); history.append(-np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p)))
